name: Volumouse
tagline: A desktop utility that turns your mouse wheel into a volume knob, with rules for when it should apply.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a single-purpose input hook: intercept scroll wheel events under some condition, map them to system volume, show feedback. There is no server, no account, no data, and nothing an agent cannot reach with a documented OS API. A one-sitting script gets you the 90 percent case, hold a modifier key and scroll anywhere to change volume, with an on-screen readout. What the paid tool actually sells is the long tail: dozens of trigger conditions, per-window rules, multiple audio channels, a config UI, and a signed installer that your IT department will not scream about. If you only ever wanted one rule, you were overpaying for 40 of them.
coreLoopDIY: A background script intercepts mouse wheel events while a chosen modifier key is held and maps them to system volume up or down with a small on-screen indicator.
requirements: A Windows machine (the equivalent macOS build needs an Accessibility permission grant and a different API)
Willingness to add the script to startup yourself
whatYouLose: Rule breadth: triggers on window titles, specific apps, screen edges, mouse buttons, keyboard states, instead of your one hardcoded modifier
Per-application and per-device volume control rather than the single system mixer
Other channels: microphone level, individual mixer lines, display brightness in some builds
A real settings GUI, so every tweak means editing code
A signed, updating installer and a tray icon that looks like someone designed it
moatNotes: The moat here is years of edge cases on weird mice, remote desktop sessions, and fullscreen games. Your script will meet all of them eventually.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody wants a maintenance project for a volume knob. The paid utility is a one-time cost, starts with Windows, survives OS updates, and has a checkbox for the exact trigger condition you want instead of a script you have to remember how to edit. People also pay to avoid the specific hell of debugging a global input hook that silently stops working after a Windows update, which is the one failure mode a DIY version will absolutely hit.
notes: One of the rare cases where the one-shot build is genuinely shorter than the app's settings dialog.
prompt:
Build a single-file Windows background utility that turns the mouse wheel into a system volume control.

Stack, no alternatives:
- AutoHotkey v2, one script file named volumouse.ahk, plus a README.md.
- No installer, no compiler step, no external libraries, no network calls, no telemetry.

Behavior:
- While the ALT key is held down, mouse wheel up raises system volume, wheel down lowers it.
- Each wheel notch changes volume by 2 percent. Make that a named constant at the top of the file.
- ALT plus middle mouse button toggles mute.
- When ALT is not held, scroll events must pass through to the focused window completely unchanged. This is the most important requirement: do not swallow normal scrolling.
- Show the current volume level and mute state as a small always-on-top overlay near the mouse cursor, which fades out about 800 ms after the last change. Build it with AutoHotkey's Gui, borderless, click-through, no taskbar entry.
- Add a tray menu with: Suspend hotkeys, Reload, Edit script, Exit.

Config:
- Put the modifier key, the step size, and the overlay timeout in clearly labeled constants at the top of the script. No settings file, no registry writes.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build:
- Per-application volume, microphone or other mixer channels, brightness control, window-title or app-specific rules, multi-monitor overlay positioning logic, auto-update.

README must cover: installing the AutoHotkey v2 runtime, running the script, adding a shortcut to shell:startup for launch on login, and a note that the overlay will not appear over exclusive-fullscreen games.

Test it by hand before declaring done: confirm normal scrolling still works in a browser, confirm ALT plus scroll changes volume in 2 percent steps, confirm the overlay disappears on its own.
